speakers.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
speakers.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: To ask His Majesty’s Government what steps they are taking to ensure the benefits of technical education are being shared and highlighted across secondary schools.
contributions.name: Lord McNicol of West Kilbride

contributions.who: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions (Baroness Smith of Malvern) (Lab)
contributions.text: My Lords, we want technical and vocational education to be valued as highly as academic study. We are co-designing new technical education routes from 14 to 16 with mayoral and strategic authorities to ensure that local skills needs are reflected, and we will work closely with schools, colleges and employers as these are developed. Schools must provide independent careers guidance from year 7 and give pupils at least six opportunities during years 8 to 13 to hear directly from apprenticeship and technical education providers.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: I thank my noble friend the Minister for her response. When polytechnics and technical colleges became universities in the early 1990s, something was lost. What was lost was a clear and respected education path whose value was understood by students, employers and parents alike. I benefited from that route at Dundee Institute of Technology, where my HND in building management laid the foundations for a career that I am proud of. Today, that pathway is less visible in our schools. I welcome the comments of my noble friend the Minister, but can she go further? Does she agree with me that careers advice should present students with the option of technical qualifications with the same weight as university degrees? If yes, what more can the Government do?
contributions.name: Lord McNicol of West Kilbride

contributions.text: I agree with my noble friend. A university degree will be the right choice for some young people, but it is not the only route to a successful career. As I have said, young people should receive impartial advice about all their options, including higher technical qualifications at levels 4 and 5, as my noble friend has identified, and should be able to hear directly from the providers delivering them. These qualifications offer a clear route into skilled work and further progression. Through careers hubs and providers, we are helping young people and their parents understand the opportunities available and make the choice that is right for them. These qualifications also feature on our Skills for Careers website and information, and from next year the lifelong learning entitlement will also enable funding to be available for level 4 and 5 courses, and modules of them, as well as for degrees.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, the Minister is rightly alluding to the necessity for us to have greater expertise in technical and engineering results in our institutions. Apprenticeships are of course necessary, but is she satisfied that employers are generally recognising the need for apprentices, and that they have the resources and the support of the Government in employing far more people in that important route?
contributions.name: Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate

contributions.text: The honest answer is no, I do not think there is enough yet—which is why we want to double down particularly on our efforts to increase the numbers of young people who are able to benefit from apprenticeships. It is why we have invested an additional £1 billion into the apprenticeship budget, why we are providing new incentives for employers to take on young people in particular as apprentices, and why we are developing a local apprenticeship service—so that, at a local level, businesses can be brought into direct contact with the benefits of offering apprenticeships, and with the young people who can benefit from them.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: Can the Minister say how the recruitment of teachers for vocational and technical education is going, and whether schools are being supplied with the goods and equipment they need to ensure that pupils have a decent chance of acquiring the skills that are so badly needed by employers?
contributions.name: Baroness Garden of Frognal

contributions.text: As we develop, for example, the technical education routes that I have outlined, we are also working with schools and with teachers’ representatives to make sure not only that the right number of teachers are in place to deliver these courses but that we are thinking about the professional development that will be necessary for those teachers. Having taught both academic and vocational subjects alongside each other, I think it is key to have qualified teachers in front of young people, to provide the tenets of good teaching—many of which spread across technical and vocational and academic teaching—to as many teachers as possible, and to meet our target for more qualified teachers in front of students, as we are successfully doing at the moment.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: What the Minister has said is admirable, but what are the Government doing to enhance the status of technical work?
contributions.name: Baroness Butler-Sloss

contributions.text: It is important that the new Prime Minister has emphasised—for example, with his proposal for new technical routes for young people from 14 to 16—the significance he places on those qualifications. In developing new vocational GCSEs, we will also boost the status of these more technical and vocational qualifications by ensuring that they are based on national standards and national content—something that does not happen at the moment with the technical awards that students take. We will ensure, particularly as we develop work with strategic authorities, that it is clear that the routes young people take through technical and vocational qualifications will lead them to high-quality destinations, whether higher education, skilled work or apprenticeships. That is what will make this education valuable in the eyes of young people and their parents.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I note my interest as one of the Government’s enrichment ambassadors. Behind every show and film made in this country are a whole host of world-class, exceptional technicians, engineers and set builders, but the theatre and film sectors tell us that these are among the hardest roles to fill. I welcome the Government’s post-16 reforms, including new creative T-levels and the enrichment expansion programme. Will the Minister outline how these developments can work together, so that a pupil who discovers backstage work through enrichment can follow a route through education and into work?
contributions.name: Lord Davey of Chalk Farm

contributions.text: My noble friend has considerable experience in this area. He is absolutely right to highlight both the opportunities available in the creative industries and the enormous contribution that those industries make to the country as a whole. That is why, as part of our post-16 qualifications reform, I have been very pleased to bring together an advisory group of those working within the creative sector and providing education in that sector to make sure that we will have the highest-quality routes for young people to be able to get some of the brilliant jobs that my noble friend identified.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, the Minister knows that I share her desire to ensure that as many young people as possible have a future route through their education. The Government have said that technical awards vary by provider, have no nationally set content and do not consistently support progression to further study. There will be a problem for one cohort in 2028: the technical pathways that start in September 2028 will use the same technical awards that the Government recognise are problematic, because the new vocational GCSEs will not be ready until 2029 at the earliest. How can schools be expected to promote qualifications that the Government themselves have called inconsistent? Will the Minister ensure that no child of the 2028 cohort is pushed into qualifications that will not lead to a post-16 route?
contributions.name: Baroness Cash

contributions.text: I share the noble Baroness’s objective that we need to keep improving the system in order to make sure that the routes available to young people are of the highest possible quality. As the noble Baroness said, we will introduce new vocational GCSEs from 2029, with nationally set content that we think will be of a higher quality than existing technical awards. We think that there are opportunities, particularly in mayoral strategic authorities, to develop routes using existing technical awards, which have brought alongside them high-quality work experience and links to employers, that local strategic authorities will be able to facilitate. That is an improvement on the existing position whereby lots of young people are taking technical awards and, to be fair, are succeeding. This strengthens the technical awards as we develop the new vocational GCSEs.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, what is the role of FE colleges in all this? I declare an interest: Shipley College is based in Saltaire. I am very conscious that a lot of 16 to 18 year-olds who would otherwise drop out of education do technical courses in FE colleges. How are the Government going to make sure that these play a very worthwhile role in developing this further?
contributions.name: Lord Wallace of Saltaire

contributions.text: The noble Lord probably shares my view that FE is the sector that has too often been overlooked in the education system. But not by this Government, which is why we have increased investment, we have enabled pay awards to be offered on the same basis as they are being offered in schools, we have invested in technical excellence colleges and we will continue to work with FE colleges to ensure that the excellent partnerships they have with employers, and the technical education in which they often excel, are not only supported but developed in the years to come.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions
